whatItIs.text: Soybeans fermented with salt and kōji (the fungus Aspergillus oryzae) into a salty-savoury paste — the backbone of miso soup and the umami reserve of the modern fridge.

historyNote.text: Fermented soy foods reached Japan from China around the sixth century with Buddhism, and 'mishō' appears in the Nara period (710-794); Buddhist monks discovered in the Muromachi era that grinding the beans into paste made something new, and by the Sengoku period miso was military rations.

howToChoose.text: White (shiro) miso is mild and sweet, red (aka) aged and punchy, awase a blend — keep one of each if you can; the ingredient list should be short, starting with soybeans, rice or barley, salt, kōji.

storage.text: Keep tightly lidded in the fridge; it darkens slowly and stays good for a very long time.

useItUp.text: Miso soup is the obvious use, but it also whips into butter for steaks, marinades fish in minutes, and deepens any stew; never boil it hard — the aroma fades.

substitutions.note: salt and umami but no body; add a little tahini for texture
